Because they often live in buildings, little brown bats are among the bats people meet most. Colonies in attics are sometimes treated as pests, and bats can carry rabies, so they should never be handled.

But one bat eats thousands of insects a night, and many people now put up bat houses to give them roosts. Caves with hibernating bats are often closed in winter, because waking bats costs them precious fat.
relatives:
The little brown bat belongs to the genus Myotis, the 'mouse-eared' bats, one of the largest and most widespread groups of mammals, with over 100 species worldwide. It closely resembles several cousins, including the endangered Indiana bat and the northern long-eared bat.

Despite its name, it is not closely related to the big brown bat, which belongs to a different genus. Experts tell the little brown bat from the Indiana bat partly by a small spur of cartilage on the edge of the wing membrane near the foot, called the calcar, which has a ridge in the Indiana bat but not in the little brown.
didYouKnow: A hibernating little brown bat may breathe only a few times a minute and wake up just once every couple of weeks.

quiz.prompt: What has killed millions of little brown bats since 2006?
choices: Very cold winters that freeze the caves where they hibernate
quiz.explanation: A fungus that grows on hibernating bats wakes them repeatedly, using up their fat.

quiz.prompt: How long can a little brown bat live?
choices: Five to six years at most
quiz.explanation: A banded bat lived about 34 years, remarkable for such a small mammal.

quiz.prompt: Where do female little brown bats raise their pups?
choices: In warm maternity colonies, often in attics
In nests woven from grass that they hang under bridges
quiz.explanation: Females gather in warm colonies in early summer, often in buildings.

charities.name: Bat Conservation International
charities.blurb: Works worldwide to protect bats and their habitats, including research on white-nose syndrome.

name: American Marten
range: Northern forests from Newfoundland to Alaska, and south into the northern US
tagline: A treetop hunter that tunnels under the snow
lede: Sleek, golden-brown and quick as a squirrel through the branches, the American marten is a small weasel of the northern forest. In winter it disappears beneath the snow, hunting voles in a hidden world of tunnels between fallen logs, and its silky fur once made it one of the most trapped animals in North America.
home:
American martens live across northern North America, from the tree line in Arctic Alaska and Canada south to New York and New England, and from Newfoundland to the Pacific coast of Canada. They depend on mature forests, especially conifer and mixed forests with plenty of fallen trees, stumps and branches near the ground.

That clutter matters in winter. Under the snow, it leaves gaps and passages where voles live, and where martens hunt, rest and shelter from the cold. Martens are scarce in young or heavily logged forest.
anatomy:
A marten is about the size of a mink, with a long, slender body, short legs, a bushy tail and large, rounded ears on a roughly triangular head. Its long, silky fur ranges from pale buff to tawny brown to almost black, with a paler head and darker legs and tail.

On its throat and chest is a 'bib' that's a different shade, often orange or cream. Males are much bigger than females, sometimes weighing about 1.5 times as much. Martens have sharp, semi-retractable claws for climbing, and furry feet that help in snow.
life:
Martens are omnivores, but they rely mostly on small mammals, especially voles. They also catch red squirrels, mice, snowshoe hares and birds, and eat eggs, insects, carrion and berries in season. They are solitary and active mostly at dawn, dusk and night, though they can be busy for 10 to 16 hours a day.

In summer they may be active more than half the day; in deep winter as little as a sixth, resting in hollow logs, squirrel middens or under the snow. When it gets colder than about minus 20 degrees, they spend more time below the snow surface, where it's warmer.
family:
Martens mate in midsummer, in July or August, but the embryo doesn't implant in the female's womb until late winter, so kits aren't born until the following spring, in March or April. A litter has one to five kits, born blind and nearly hairless in a den in a hollow tree, log or rock pile.

The mother moves them between dens as they grow, and they stay with her until autumn. Young martens are mature by a year old, though most don't breed until they're two. In the wild, females as old as 12 have still had young.
remarkable: Martens are agile enough to chase red squirrels through the treetops, leaping from branch to branch, and can climb down trunks head-first. They spend much of their hunting time, though, on the ground and beneath the snow.
outlook:
The American marten is listed as Least Concern, and its numbers have recovered across much of its range.

It is still missing from some areas where it once lived, and local populations depend on old forest. In Newfoundland, the island's isolated marten population fell to a few hundred and is protected.
people:
With fur as soft as Eurasian sable, the American marten was one of the most valuable animals of the North American fur trade. Trapping peaked around 1820, and populations stayed low until well into the 20th century, when trapping rules and reintroductions helped them recover.

Martens are still trapped legally in much of Canada and Alaska. Because they need old, structurally complex forests, wildlife managers often use them as an indicator of forest health.
relatives:
The American marten is a mustelid, a member of the weasel family, along with fishers, minks, otters, badgers and wolverines. It is closely related to the Eurasian pine marten and the sable of Siberia.

The Pacific marten, of the Pacific Northwest and California, was once thought to be the same species, but genetic studies show it is separate, with a longer snout and broader skull. The fisher looks similar but is bigger and darker.
didYouKnow: Martens are so dependent on old forests that a whole area of trees can be judged healthy or not by whether martens live there.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Mostly voles and other small mammals

quiz.prompt: Where does an American marten hunt in winter?
choices: In gaps and tunnels under the snow
Around farms, where it raids chicken coops for food
quiz.explanation: Fallen logs and branches leave spaces under the snow where voles live and martens hunt.

quiz.prompt: What is the 'bib' on a marten?
choices: A patch of different-coloured fur on its throat
A flap of skin for gliding
A thick ring of fat around the neck that keeps it warm
quiz.explanation: Martens have a throat and chest patch, often orange or cream, that differs from the rest of the coat.

quiz.prompt: Why was the American marten heavily trapped?
choices: Because it damaged trees in logging forests across Canada
quiz.explanation: Its sable-like fur made it one of the most valuable animals in the fur trade, which peaked around 1820.

charities.name: Canadian Wildlife Federation
charities.blurb: Works to conserve Canada's wildlife and habitats through research, education and restoration.

name: American Pika
range: Rocky mountain slopes of western North America, from British Columbia to New Mexico
tagline: A tiny hay farmer of the high mountains
lede: High on mountain rock slides, a small round animal with no visible tail scurries back and forth with mouthfuls of flowers. The American pika doesn't hibernate; instead, it spends the short alpine summer making hay, building piles of dried plants to eat through the long winter under the snow.
home:
American pikas live in the mountains of western North America, from central British Columbia and Alberta south through the Rockies, Cascades and Sierra Nevada to New Mexico and California.

They live almost exclusively in talus, the fields of broken rock that pile up below cliffs, usually at or above the tree line, next to meadows where they gather food. The gaps between boulders give shelter from predators and from heat. Pikas need cool conditions, and in the south of their range they are found only at high elevations.
anatomy:
An American pika is about 16 to 22 centimetres long and weighs 121 to 176 grams, about the weight of a large apple. It is egg-shaped and compact, with short legs, rounded ears and no visible tail, which helps it hold in heat.

Its fur is greyish brown to buff, thick and soft. The soles of its feet are furry, giving it grip on smooth rock. Pikas were once called 'little chief hares', and although they look like rodents, they are close relatives of rabbits and hares.
life:
Pikas are active by day, unusual for an animal their size. They eat a wide range of plants: grasses, sedges, thistles, fireweed and wildflowers. In late summer they 'go haying', making up to dozens of trips an hour to carry stems and flowers back to haypiles tucked under boulders.

Some haypiles grow large enough to fill a bathtub. Each pika defends a territory of about 410 to 709 square metres, with neighbouring pairs living closer together than pikas of the same sex. They are noisy, using short calls to warn of eagles, hawks, coyotes, foxes and weasels, and longer songs in the breeding season.
family:
Pikas with neighbouring territories pair up, and females may choose between several males. Breeding starts about a month before the snow melts, and after a pregnancy of about 30 days, the female gives birth, as early as March at lower elevations.

Females usually have two litters a year, each averaging three young, though the second litter often fails. The young grow fast and must claim a territory and build a haypile of their own before their first winter.
remarkable:
Pikas can't cope with heat. They have a high body temperature and thick fur, and can die after a few hours in temperatures of around 25 degrees if they can't find cool shade.

On hot days they shelter deep in the rocks, where the air stays cool.
outlook:
The American pika is listed as Least Concern overall, and it is still common in the northern Rockies and Canada. But it is considered an early warning sign of climate change.

In parts of the Great Basin in Nevada and Utah, pikas have disappeared from lower sites, and warming pushes the survivors higher up mountains, where there is less room and nowhere higher to go.
people:
Pikas are popular with hikers, who often hear their sharp 'eep' calls from rock slides before spotting them.

Because they are easy to survey by listening for calls and looking for haypiles, volunteer projects across the western US and Canada help scientists track where pikas still live and where they have vanished. The naturalist John Richardson first described the species for science in 1828.
relatives:
Pikas are lagomorphs, the order that includes rabbits and hares. There are about 30 species of pika, most in the mountains and steppes of Asia; the American pika is one of only two in North America, along with the collared pika of Alaska and northwestern Canada.

Like rabbits, pikas have a second, smaller pair of upper front teeth tucked behind the first, which is one way to tell lagomorphs from rodents.
didYouKnow: An American pika may make more than a dozen trips an hour, all summer, to fill its winter haypile.

quiz.prompt: How does the American pika survive the winter?
choices: It eats hay it stored in summer
It hibernates in a burrow until spring
quiz.explanation: Pikas don't hibernate; they live on haypiles of plants gathered in late summer.

quiz.prompt: Which animals are pikas most closely related to?
choices: Marmots and groundhogs, which share their rocky homes
quiz.explanation: Pikas are lagomorphs, like rabbits and hares, not rodents.

quiz.prompt: Why are pikas called a warning sign of climate change?
choices: They eat plants that only grow in warm years
They breed faster when it's warm
They need deep snow to hibernate
quiz.explanation: Pikas overheat easily and are disappearing from lower, warmer sites.

charities.name: Nature Conservancy of Canada
charities.blurb: Protects natural areas across Canada, including mountain habitats in British Columbia and Alberta.

name: Black-footed Ferret
range: Prairie dog colonies of the North American Great Plains
tagline: Declared extinct, then found by a farm dog
lede: In 1979 the black-footed ferret was declared extinct. Two years later, a last few turned up on a Wyoming ranch. From that last colony came one of the most dramatic rescues in conservation: every black-footed ferret alive today descends from just a handful of survivors, and one of them is a clone.
home:
Black-footed ferrets live on the short-grass and mixed-grass prairies of the Great Plains, and they depend completely on prairie dogs. They live in prairie dog colonies, sleep and raise young in prairie dog burrows, and eat prairie dogs.

Their historical range stretched from southern Alberta and Saskatchewan south to Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, matching the range of prairie dogs. Today they live only at reintroduction sites in the western United States, Canada and Mexico.
anatomy:
The black-footed ferret is a slender weasel, about 50 to 60 centimetres long including its tail, with a long neck and short, stout legs.

Its fur is buff or tan, with black feet, a black tip to the tail, and a black mask across the eyes. It has a broad, arched forehead, a short muzzle, few whiskers and large triangular ears. Its long, narrow body is perfectly shaped for slipping down prairie dog burrows.
life:
Black-footed ferrets are solitary and nocturnal, and spend most of their time underground. They are most active above ground from dusk to midnight and again before dawn. Up to 90 percent of their diet is prairie dogs, which they usually catch asleep in their burrows; the rest is mice, ground squirrels and rabbits. A single ferret eats over 100 prairie dogs a year, so a family needs a large colony to survive.

Their own predators include coyotes, badgers, great horned owls and golden eagles. They are expert diggers too, clearing soil out of burrows and leaving telltale trenches of dirt on the surface, one of the signs biologists look for when searching for ferrets at night with spotlights.
family:
Ferrets mate in February and March. After about six weeks, the female gives birth to a litter of usually three or four kits in a prairie dog burrow. The kits stay underground until they are about two months old.

By late summer and early autumn, the young become independent and disperse, the time when ferrets are most visible above ground. Life in the wild is hard: many ferrets live only about a year.
remarkable: In 2021, scientists announced the first cloned black-footed ferret, a female named Elizabeth Ann, made from cells frozen in the 1980s from a ferret called Willa, whose genes had been lost from the living population. Her clone sisters, Noreen and Antonia, followed, and in 2024 Antonia gave birth to kits.
outlook:
The black-footed ferret is listed as endangered. It was moved to 'extinct in the wild' in 1996 and back to endangered in 2008 after reintroductions. About 300 live in the wild, with a few self-sustaining populations in South Dakota, Arizona and Wyoming.

The biggest threats are sylvatic plague, a disease introduced from Asia that kills both ferrets and prairie dogs, and the loss and poisoning of prairie dog colonies. Biologists dust prairie dog burrows to kill the fleas that spread plague.
people:
Native American nations, including the Crow, Blackfoot, Sioux, Cheyenne and Pawnee, used black-footed ferrets in religious rites. Lewis and Clark never saw one, and the species wasn't described by science until John James Audubon and John Bachman did so in 1851.

As prairies were ploughed and prairie dogs poisoned as pests through the 20th century, ferrets vanished with them. In 1981, a dog named Shep brought a dead ferret home to a ranch near Meeteetse, Wyoming, revealing the last wild colony. After disease struck it, the last 18 ferrets were taken into captivity in 1987 to start a breeding programme.
relatives:
The black-footed ferret is a member of the weasel family and North America's only native ferret.

Its closest relative is the steppe polecat of Asia, and both descend from a European ancestor that crossed into North America over the Bering land bridge. The domestic ferret is a descendant of the European polecat, not of the black-footed ferret.
didYouKnow: Every black-footed ferret alive today descends from just seven of the 18 animals rescued in Wyoming in the 1980s.

quiz.prompt: What makes up most of a black-footed ferret's diet?
quiz.explanation: Up to 90 percent of its diet is prairie dogs, and it lives in their burrows.

quiz.prompt: How was the last wild colony discovered in 1981?
choices: A ranch dog brought home a dead ferret
A biologist found tracks in the snow near Meeteetse
It was seen on a TV news report
quiz.explanation: A dog named Shep brought a ferret home near Meeteetse, Wyoming.

quiz.prompt: What disease is one of the biggest threats to black-footed ferrets?
quiz.explanation: Plague, introduced from Asia, kills both ferrets and the prairie dogs they depend on.

charities.name: World Wildlife Fund
charities.blurb: Works with ranchers and tribes on the Northern Great Plains to restore prairies, prairie dogs and black-footed ferrets.

name: Walrus
range: Arctic and subarctic seas, from the Bering Sea to Hudson Bay, Greenland and Svalbard
tagline: Tusks, whiskers and 2 tonnes of blubber
lede: A walrus uses its tusks to haul itself out of the sea, its whiskers to feel for clams in the dark, and its mouth like a vacuum to suck them out of their shells. Pacific bulls can top 2 tonnes, and in late summer tens of thousands crowd onto Arctic beaches together.
home:
Walruses live around the North Pole in the Arctic Ocean and nearby seas. Pacific walruses spend the winter in the Bering Sea and migrate north into the Chukchi Sea in spring and summer, several hundred thousand animals following the ice.

Atlantic walruses live from the Canadian Arctic and Hudson Bay to Greenland, Svalbard and northern Russia. They prefer shallow water over the continental shelf, where they can reach the seafloor, and rest on floating sea ice between dives. When the ice melts back, they haul out on rocky beaches instead.
anatomy:
Walruses are huge: most Pacific bulls weigh 800 to 1,700 kg, and some more than 2,000 kg. Only the two elephant seals are bigger among seals and sea lions. Their skin is wrinkled and nearly hairless, up to 10 centimetres thick on a bull's neck and shoulders, over a layer of blubber up to 15 centimetres deep.

Young walruses are deep brown and grow paler and more cinnamon with age. Both sexes have tusks, which are long canine teeth that can reach 1 metre and weigh more than 5 kg; males' are longer and thicker. Around the mouth grow 400 to 700 stiff, sensitive whiskers in rows, up to 30 centimetres long.
life:
Walruses feed mostly on clams and other shellfish on the seafloor, usually in water less than 80 metres deep. They don't dig with their tusks. Instead they search with their whiskers, then blow jets of water or suck with their powerful mouths to expose clams and pull the soft bodies out of their shells.

They also eat worms, snails, sea cucumbers and, occasionally, seals. Walruses are very social. They use their tusks to climb out onto ice, to defend themselves against polar bears and orcas, and to establish rank: the walrus with the biggest tusks usually wins.
family:
Bulls reach maturity as early as 7 years old but usually don't mate until they're fully grown, at around 15. In winter, they display to females in the water, making whistles, knocks and bell-like sounds, and fight rivals with their tusks.

A female gives birth to a single calf, usually every three years, after a pregnancy of about 15 months. Calves can swim at birth and stay with their mothers for two years or more, a long time for a seal. Walruses live 20 to 30 years in the wild.
remarkable: A walrus can suck so hard that it pulls a clam out of its shell in seconds, and can eat thousands of clams in a single feeding session. When resting at sea, it can inflate air sacs in its throat to float upright and sleep with its head above water.
outlook:
The walrus is listed as Vulnerable. Commercial hunting in the 19th and early 20th centuries for blubber, ivory and leather crashed numbers all around the Arctic, and Atlantic walruses still live in small, scattered groups.

The biggest threat now is the loss of sea ice. Without ice over shallow feeding grounds, walruses crowd onto beaches by the tens of thousands, where stampedes set off by planes, boats or polar bears can crush calves.
people:
Walruses have been central to many Arctic Indigenous cultures, which still hunt them for meat, fat, skin and ivory, used for tools and carving.

Hunting by Indigenous communities continues under co-management rules in Alaska, Canada, Greenland and Russia. The oldest known walrus was Slowpoke, who lived to 49 at SeaWorld Orlando.
relatives:
The walrus is the only living member of its family, Odobenidae, one of three groups of pinnipeds along with true seals and eared seals, such as sea lions.

Its closest relatives are the eared seals. Fossils show many extinct walrus relatives, including some without long tusks. The two living subspecies are the Atlantic walrus and the Pacific walrus, which is larger.
didYouKnow: Walruses use their tusks to haul themselves out of the water onto ice, and their scientific family name, Odobenidae, means 'tooth-walkers'.

quiz.prompt: How does a walrus find clams on the dark seafloor?
choices: By watching for bubbles that clams give off as they breathe
quiz.explanation: It feels for prey with hundreds of stiff whiskers, then sucks the clams from their shells.

quiz.prompt: What are walrus tusks?
choices: Hardened whiskers that grow back every year
quiz.explanation: Tusks are elongated canine teeth, found in both males and females.

quiz.prompt: Why are walruses gathering on beaches in huge numbers?
choices: The sea ice they rest on is disappearing
The water is too warm to swim in
quiz.explanation: Without ice over their feeding grounds, they haul out on land, where stampedes can crush calves.

charities.name: World Wildlife Fund
charities.blurb: Works with Arctic communities to protect walruses and other wildlife as sea ice declines.

name: Sea Otter
range: North Pacific coasts, from Japan and Russia through Alaska to California
tagline: The thickest fur in the animal kingdom
lede: Floating on its back in a kelp forest, cracking a clam on a rock balanced on its chest, the sea otter is one of the few animals that use tools. It has no blubber to keep warm, so it relies on the densest fur of any animal, and by eating sea urchins it keeps entire kelp forests alive.
home:
Sea otters live along the coasts of the North Pacific, from northern Japan and Russia's Kuril and Commander Islands through the Aleutian Islands and Alaska, down British Columbia and Washington to California.

They stay close to shore, usually within a kilometre or two, in water shallow enough to dive to the seafloor. Many live in kelp forests, where they wrap themselves in kelp fronds to keep from drifting away while they sleep.
anatomy:
Sea otters are the heaviest members of the weasel family but among the smallest marine mammals. Males weigh 22 to 45 kg and are 1.2 to 1.5 metres long; females are smaller. Instead of blubber, they are kept warm by fur with 100,000 to 400,000 hairs per square centimetre, trapping a layer of air against the skin. They must groom constantly to keep it clean and waterproof.

Their hind feet are broad, webbed flippers, and their front paws have retractable claws and tough pads for gripping slippery prey. Under each foreleg is a loose pouch of skin where they store food and a favourite rock.
life:
Sea otters feed in short dives to the seafloor, usually lasting about a minute, though they can hold their breath for up to five. They eat sea urchins, clams, mussels, crabs, snails and some fish, and they can flip over rocks with their paws to find them.

To open hard shells, an otter floats on its back with a rock on its chest and bashes the prey against it. To stay warm in cold water, it has to eat about a quarter of its body weight every day. Otters feed in the morning and afternoon, rest at midday and often feed again around midnight.
family:
Males defend territories and mate with the females that live there. After mating, a female gives birth to a single pup, usually in the water.

The pup's fur is so fluffy and full of air that it can't dive; it floats like a cork while its mother hunts. The mother carries the pup on her chest, grooms it and nurses it for about six months, teaching it to dive and use tools.
remarkable:
Sea otters are a keystone species. By eating sea urchins, they stop urchins from grazing kelp forests down to bare rock.

Where otters disappeared, kelp forests collapsed into 'urchin barrens'; where they returned, the kelp, and the fish and other life it shelters, came back.
outlook:
The sea otter is listed as endangered. Hunting for their fur between 1741 and 1911 reduced a population of perhaps 150,000 to 300,000 to just 1,000 to 2,000 animals in a few scattered places. An international hunting ban in 1911, protection and reintroductions brought them back to much of their range, including British Columbia.

But numbers in the Aleutians fell sharply from the 1990s, possibly because orcas began eating them, and oil spills, disease and conflicts with shellfish fisheries remain threats.
people:
Sea otter fur was the most valuable in the 18th and 19th centuries, driving Russian, British and American traders across the North Pacific. Their hunt shaped the history of Alaska and the Northwest Coast.

Today, otters are a draw for wildlife watchers, and the Monterey Bay Aquarium has raised orphaned pups with surrogate otter mothers to return them to the wild.
relatives: The sea otter is the only living member of its genus, Enhydra, and part of the otter subfamily of the weasel family, along with 13 other otter species, from the giant otter of the Amazon to the North American river otter. It is the only mustelid with no functional scent glands, and the only one able to spend its whole life at sea without coming ashore.
didYouKnow: Sea otters sometimes hold hands while they sleep, or wrap themselves in kelp, so they don't drift apart.

quiz.prompt: How does a sea otter stay warm without blubber?
choices: Its fur is the densest of any animal
It basks on rocks all day
It sleeps curled up in underwater caves between the kelp
quiz.explanation: Its fur, with up to 400,000 hairs per square centimetre, traps a layer of insulating air.

quiz.prompt: How do sea otters help kelp forests?
choices: They eat sea urchins that graze on kelp
They clean the kelp with their paws
quiz.explanation: Without otters, urchins can graze kelp forests down to bare rock.

quiz.prompt: What does a sea otter use a rock for?
choices: To crack open shellfish on its chest
To scratch its fur when it gets dirty
quiz.explanation: It floats on its back with a rock on its chest and bashes shellfish against it.

charities.name: Monterey Bay Aquarium
charities.blurb: Runs a sea otter research and rescue programme and works to protect ocean habitats.

name: Snowy Owl
range: Arctic tundra around the North Pole; winters south into Canada and the northern US
tagline: The Arctic's white hunter of the midnight sun
lede: The only owl that is mostly white, the snowy owl is the largest bird of prey of the high Arctic. It hunts in the round-the-clock daylight of the tundra summer, and in some winters, flocks of them fly south and turn up on airports, beaches and farm fields from Canada to Texas.
home:
Snowy owls breed on the open Arctic tundra around the North Pole, usually north of 60 degrees latitude, in Alaska, northern Canada, Greenland, Scandinavia and Russia. They are nomads: where they nest each year depends on where lemmings are plentiful. In winter, many move south.

They prefer wide-open country that resembles the tundra, such as prairies, shorelines, marshes, farm fields and airports. In some years, called irruptions, unusually large numbers spread across southern Canada and the northern United States, and a few reach much farther south.
anatomy:
This is one of the largest owls in the world, and the heaviest bird of prey in the high Arctic. It has a round head with bright yellow eyes and, usually, no visible ear tufts. Males are almost pure white; females and young birds are flecked and barred with dark brown, which helps hide them on the nest.

Their feathers are extremely thick and long, covering even their feet and toes like fluffy slippers, and their dense plumage makes them one of the heaviest owls for their size. Standing on the ground, a snowy owl can look like a pale rock or a lump of snow.
life:
Unlike most owls, snowy owls are often active by day, which is necessary in an Arctic summer with no darkness at all. On the breeding grounds they hunt mainly lemmings, and an adult may eat several a day. In other seasons they take almost any prey they can find: voles, hares, ptarmigan, ducks, seabirds and even carrion.

They usually hunt by sitting on a low rise and watching, then flying low to snatch prey from the ground, the water or the air. Their main call is a deep, barking hoot, and scientists have recorded as many as 15 different calls.
family:
Snowy owls nest on the ground, usually on a small rise with a good view, where the female scrapes a shallow hollow. When lemmings are abundant, a female may lay a very large clutch, often 3 to 11 eggs, laid over several days, so the chicks hatch at different times.

In years with few lemmings, many don't breed at all. The female incubates while the male hunts for both of them, and the male defends the nest fiercely, diving at Arctic foxes, wolves and even people. The chicks leave the nest before they can fly and scatter across the tundra while their parents keep feeding them.
remarkable: Satellite tracking has shown that snowy owls wander enormous distances, and that some spend the winter far out on the frozen Arctic Ocean, hunting seabirds in open leads in the sea ice, during weeks of near-total darkness.
outlook: The snowy owl was listed as Vulnerable in 2017, after studies suggested the global population was far smaller than once thought and may be declining. Climate change threatens the tundra and its lemming cycles, and in the south, owls are killed by collisions with vehicles, planes and power lines.
people:
Snowy owls have long been important to Arctic peoples, and appear in Inuit stories and art. The snowy owl is the official bird of Quebec.

In the Harry Potter books and films, Harry's owl Hedwig is a snowy owl, which brought the species worldwide fame. Winter irruptions draw crowds of birdwatchers. At some airports, where owls are drawn to the open grassland, they are trapped and moved to safer places rather than harmed.
relatives:
The snowy owl belongs to the genus Bubo, the horned owls and eagle-owls, which includes the great horned owl of the Americas and the Eurasian eagle-owl.

It was once placed in its own genus, Nyctea, but genetic studies show it is a close relative of the great horned owl. Its scientific name, scandiacus, means 'of Scandinavia'. Carl Linnaeus described it in 1758.
didYouKnow: Male snowy owls tend to get whiter as they age, and some very old males are almost pure white.

quiz.prompt: Why are snowy owls often active during the day?
choices: They can't see well at night
Their prey only comes out at noon
They need sunlight to keep their eggs warm on the ground
quiz.explanation: In the tundra summer the sun never sets, so they hunt in daylight.

quiz.prompt: What decides how many eggs a snowy owl lays?
choices: How many owls nest nearby on the same patch of tundra
quiz.explanation: In lemming-rich years clutches are large; when lemmings crash, many don't breed.

quiz.prompt: How can you tell a male snowy owl from a female?
quiz.explanation: Males are nearly pure white, while females have more dark brown flecks and bars.

charities.name: Project SNOWstorm
charities.blurb: Tracks snowy owls with GPS transmitters to learn how they move and survive in winter.

name: Humpback Whale
range: Oceans worldwide, migrating between polar feeding grounds and tropical breeding waters
tagline: The singing whale that hunts with nets of bubbles
lede: A 40-tonne humpback whale can launch its whole body out of the sea, sing songs that last half an hour, and catch fish by blowing a spiral net of bubbles. Hunted almost to extinction in the 20th century, it has made one of the greatest comebacks in the ocean.
home:
Humpback whales live in every ocean. Most make long seasonal migrations, among the longest of any mammal: they spend the summer feeding in cold, food-rich waters towards the poles, then travel to warm, shallow tropical waters to breed and give birth in winter.

In the North Atlantic, humpbacks feed off Newfoundland, the Gulf of St. Lawrence, Iceland and Norway, and breed in the Caribbean. Pacific humpbacks feed off Alaska and British Columbia and breed around Hawaii and Mexico. Southern Hemisphere humpbacks feed in Antarctic waters.
anatomy:
Adults are usually 14 to 15 metres long, and can reach 17 metres and 40 tonnes. Females are a little longer than males. A humpback has a stocky body, a small dorsal fin on a hump, which gives it its name, and knobbly bumps called tubercles on its head and jaw, each with a stiff hair.

Its flippers are the longest of any whale, up to a third of its body length, and its scientific name, Megaptera, means 'big wing'. The underside of its tail flukes has a black and white pattern unique to each whale, which researchers use to identify individuals. Instead of teeth, it has baleen plates for straining food.
life:
Humpbacks feed from spring to autumn, mainly on krill and small schooling fish such as herring, capelin and sand lance. They often feed in groups, using a technique called bubble-netting: one or more whales swim in a spiral below a shoal, blowing bubbles that rise around the fish like a curtain, then the whales lunge up through the middle with their mouths wide open.

They are very active at the surface, leaping clear of the water, a move called breaching, and slapping the sea with their flippers and tails. Apart from mothers and calves, groups usually stay together for only days or weeks. Humpbacks often carry passengers: barnacles and whale lice cling to their skin, especially on the head and flippers.
family:
Humpbacks mate in their winter breeding grounds, where both sexes have several partners. Males follow females and fight rivals by charging, ramming and slapping. After a pregnancy of about 11 months, the female gives birth in warm, shallow water to a single calf about 4 metres long.

The calf drinks rich milk and grows quickly, then makes the long migration to the feeding grounds beside its mother. Orcas are the humpback's main natural predator, and mothers and other adults escort calves to protect them.
remarkable: Male humpbacks sing long, complex songs during the breeding season, lasting 4 to 33 minutes and repeated for hours. All the males in a population sing the same song, which slowly changes over the season, and new songs can spread from one ocean region to another, like a hit tune.
outlook:
The humpback whale is listed as Least Concern. Commercial whaling reduced the world population to about 5,000 by the 1960s, before a ban on hunting humpbacks in 1966.

Numbers have since recovered to about 135,000. Entanglement in fishing gear, collisions with ships and noise pollution still kill and injure many.
people:
Humpbacks were among the most heavily hunted whales because they swim slowly and stay close to coasts. The 1970 album 'Songs of the Humpback Whale', made from underwater recordings, became a bestseller and helped launch the worldwide campaign to save whales.

Today humpbacks are the stars of whale watching, from Newfoundland and Quebec to Hawaii and Australia.
relatives:
The humpback is a rorqual, part of the family Balaenopteridae, which includes the blue whale, fin whale and minke whales. Rorquals have pleated throats that expand like a balloon to gulp huge mouthfuls of water and prey.

It is the only species in its genus. Its species name, novaeangliae, means 'of New England', where early specimens were described.
didYouKnow: A humpback's song can be heard at least 10 kilometres away underwater.

quiz.prompt: What is bubble-netting?
choices: Trapping fish inside a ring of rising bubbles
Making a bubble nest for a calf to rest in at the surface
quiz.explanation: Humpbacks blow a spiral of bubbles around a shoal, then lunge up through the middle.

quiz.prompt: Who sings the famous humpback songs?
quiz.explanation: Males sing long, complex songs in the breeding season, and all males in a population sing the same song.

quiz.prompt: How do researchers tell individual humpbacks apart?
choices: By the pattern under their tail
By the shape of their teeth
By the length of their flippers
By the sound of their breathing at the surface
quiz.explanation: The black and white pattern under each whale's tail flukes is unique.

charities.name: Whale and Dolphin Conservation
charities.blurb: A global charity working to stop whaling, entanglement and other threats to whales and dolphins.

name: Coyote
range: Almost all of North America, from Alaska to Panama
tagline: The trickster that moved into the cities
lede: Five hundred years ago, coyotes lived mainly on the open plains and deserts of the West. Today they live in almost every corner of North America, from Alaska to Panama, including the middle of Chicago, Los Angeles and Toronto. Few animals have adapted so well to a world reshaped by people.
home:
When Europeans arrived in the Americas, coyotes were found mostly on the prairies and in the dry regions of the western half of the continent.

As forests were cleared and wolves were killed off, they spread east and north, reaching the Atlantic coast, northern Canada and Alaska. They also spread south, through Central America, and were first seen across the Panama Canal in 2013. Today they live in almost every habitat: deserts, mountains, forests, prairies, farmland, suburbs and big cities.
anatomy:
A coyote looks like a slim, smaller wolf, with large pointed ears, a narrow muzzle and a bushy, black-tipped tail that it carries low. Males usually weigh 8 to 20 kg and females 7 to 18 kg. Northern coyotes average about 18 kg, larger than those in Mexico, which average about 11.5 kg.

Its fur is mostly light grey and reddish brown, mixed with black and white, and varies across its range. Coyotes in the Northeast are larger, partly because many have some wolf ancestry from interbreeding as they spread east.
life:
Coyotes are opportunists. They eat rabbits, hares, rodents, deer, birds, reptiles, fish, insects and carrion, plus fruit and vegetables. A coyote often hunts mice by pouncing high and landing on them with its front paws, like a fox. Pairs or groups can bring down deer, especially fawns or in deep snow.

Their social life is flexible. Many live as family groups, a breeding pair with their offspring, while others live alone or in loose packs. Territories range from under 1 square kilometre to more than 60, depending on food. Their famous howls and yips help family members keep in touch and warn others off.
family:
Coyote pairs often stay together for several years. They mate in late winter, and after a pregnancy of about two months, the female gives birth in a den, often an old burrow dug by a badger or fox, a rock crevice or a hollow log.

A litter usually has about four to seven pups. Both parents bring food, and older offspring sometimes help. The pups emerge from the den at about three weeks, and many leave home in autumn, sometimes travelling more than 100 kilometres to find a territory of their own.
remarkable: When coyotes are heavily hunted or trapped, the survivors respond by having bigger litters and breeding younger, so populations bounce back quickly. Decades of efforts to kill coyotes failed to stop them spreading across the continent.
outlook:
The coyote is listed as Least Concern, and it is more widespread and numerous than ever.

Its main threats come from people: hunting, trapping and traffic. In cities, conflicts arise when coyotes lose their fear of people, usually because they've been fed.
people:
Coyote is one of the great characters of Indigenous stories across North America, a clever, foolish and sometimes creative trickster. The name 'coyote' comes from 'coyotl' in Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs and of many people in central Mexico today.

Ranchers have long seen coyotes as a threat to sheep and other livestock, and government programmes have killed millions. In cities, studies of urban coyotes show they mostly eat rodents and rabbits and avoid people, often travelling at night along rail lines and ravines.
relatives:
The coyote is a member of the dog family, closely related to the grey wolf, the eastern wolf, the red wolf and the domestic dog. In fact, these species can interbreed, and many eastern coyotes carry wolf and dog genes.

Coyote-like ancestors of the genus Canis first appeared in North America more than 5 million years ago, and the coyote itself is often described as a living example of what early wolves looked like.
didYouKnow: A coyote can run at up to about 65 km/h, fast enough to catch a jackrabbit.

quiz.prompt: Where did coyotes mainly live before Europeans arrived?
choices: The plains and dry lands of the West
The swamps of Florida and the Gulf Coast
quiz.explanation: They were mostly found in the western half of the continent before spreading east and north.

quiz.prompt: What happens when coyotes are heavily hunted?
choices: They move into the treetops to hide from hunters at night
quiz.explanation: They breed younger and have more pups, so numbers recover quickly.

quiz.prompt: Where does the word 'coyote' come from?
choices: Latin, from a word for 'barking dog' used by explorers
quiz.explanation: It comes from 'coyotl' in Nahuatl, spoken in central Mexico.

charities.name: Project Coyote
charities.blurb: Promotes coexistence between people and coyotes and other wild carnivores.

name: Bald Eagle
range: Lakes, rivers and coasts across Canada, Alaska, the US and northern Mexico
tagline: The eagle that builds a one-tonne nest
lede: The bald eagle isn't bald. Its name comes from an old meaning of the word: white-headed. North America's only native sea eagle builds the biggest tree nests ever recorded, and after nearly vanishing from the lower 48 US states, it has made one of the great conservation comebacks.
home:
Bald eagles live across most of North America: nearly all of Canada and Alaska, the contiguous United States and northern Mexico. They are found from the bayous of Louisiana and the Sonoran Desert to the forests of Quebec and New England. They need water.

They nest near seacoasts, rivers, big lakes and marshes with plenty of fish, and with tall old trees for nesting. Northern birds migrate south in winter, and many gather where water stays open, sometimes in hundreds, below dams or at salmon runs.
anatomy:
An adult bald eagle is dark brown with a white head and tail and a large, hooked yellow beak, yellow feet and pale yellow eyes. Females are about 25 percent larger than males. Wingspans range from about 1.8 to 2.3 metres.

Young eagles are mottled brown and white and don't get their white head and tail until they are four or five years old, when they're ready to breed. Their feet have rough pads on the toes, called spicules, which help them grip slippery fish.
life:
Fish make up more than half the bald eagle's diet. It snatches them from near the surface with its talons in a swooping glide, rather than plunging in. Birds, mostly waterbirds, and mammals make up much of the rest, and more than 400 species have been recorded as prey.

Bald eagles are also skilled thieves and scavengers. They eat carrion, gather at fish-processing plants and garbage dumps, and often chase ospreys and other birds to steal their catch. They soar on rising warm air, cruise at about 56 to 70 km/h and can dive at up to 160 km/h.
family:
Bald eagles usually mate for life. A pair builds a huge nest of sticks in a tall tree near water and adds to it every year. The female lays one to three eggs, and both parents incubate them for about 35 days.

The chicks fledge after about 10 to 12 weeks, but stay near the nest for several more weeks while they learn to hunt. The first-hatched chick often gets more food, and in poor years the youngest may not survive.
remarkable: Because pairs keep adding to the same nest year after year, bald eagle nests become enormous, up to 4 metres deep, 2.5 metres across and about a tonne in weight, the largest tree nests ever recorded for any animal.
outlook:
The bald eagle is listed as Least Concern. In the mid-20th century it nearly disappeared from the contiguous United States, killed by hunting, habitat loss and especially the pesticide DDT, which made eggshells so thin they broke under the parents.

DDT was banned in the US in 1972, and the eagle was protected. It recovered so well that it was removed from the US endangered species list in 2007. Lead poisoning, from eating carcasses containing bullet fragments, is still a major cause of death.
people:
The bald eagle is the national bird and symbol of the United States, chosen for the Great Seal in 1782. It is also sacred to many Indigenous peoples, and its feathers are used in ceremonies; in the US, only enrolled members of federally recognised tribes may legally hold eagle feathers.

Winter eagle gatherings, such as on the Squamish River in British Columbia and the Chilkat River in Alaska, draw thousands of visitors.
relatives:
The bald eagle is a sea eagle, genus Haliaeetus, and forms a pair with the white-tailed eagle of Europe and Asia, which fills the same role there.

Other relatives include Steller's sea eagle of Russia and Japan and the African fish eagle. Sea eagles are not closely related to golden eagles, which belong to a different group of 'booted' eagles with feathered legs.
didYouKnow: A bald eagle's feathers weigh about twice as much as its skeleton.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Mostly fish, also birds and carrion

quiz.prompt: Why is the bald eagle called 'bald'?
choices: An old meaning of 'bald' was white-headed
Young eagles have no head feathers
It loses its head feathers in winter
Its head is covered in bare, wrinkled yellow skin
quiz.explanation: 'Bald' once meant 'white-headed', describing the adult's white head feathers.

quiz.prompt: What nearly wiped out bald eagles in the 20th century?
choices: The pesticide DDT, which thinned eggshells
Competition from golden eagles that moved east
quiz.explanation: DDT made eggshells break; after it was banned in 1972, eagles recovered.

quiz.prompt: How does a bald eagle usually catch fish?
choices: Snatching them from the surface with its talons
Using its beak to spear them
quiz.explanation: It swoops low and grabs fish near the surface rather than plunging in.

charities.name: American Eagle Foundation
charities.blurb: Works to protect bald eagles and other birds of prey through rescue, education and research.

name: Peregrine Falcon
range: Every continent except Antarctica, from Arctic tundra to tropical coasts and city centres
tagline: The fastest animal on Earth, in a dive
lede: When a peregrine falcon folds its wings and drops onto a pigeon from high above, it may hit over 320 km/h, making it the fastest animal on the planet. Driven nearly to extinction by pesticides, it has bounced back, and now nests on skyscrapers in many of the world's biggest cities.
home:
The peregrine is found almost everywhere on Earth, from the Arctic tundra to the tropics, missing only from extreme polar regions, high mountains, most rainforests and, among large ice-free landmasses, New Zealand. That makes it the world's most widespread bird of prey.

It lives mostly along mountain ranges, river valleys, coastlines and, increasingly, cities, where skyscrapers, bridges and cathedrals stand in for cliffs. Peregrines that breed in the Arctic migrate long distances; those in milder places often stay on their territory all year.
anatomy:
A peregrine is about the size of a crow: 34 to 58 centimetres long, with a wingspan of 74 to 120 centimetres. Females are up to 30 percent larger than males. Adults have a blue-grey back, pale underparts finely barred with black, and a black head with a dark 'moustache' stripe below each eye.

Its long, pointed wings and stiff tail are built for speed. Small bony tubercles in its nostrils are thought to deflect the rush of air during a high-speed dive, so the falcon can keep breathing, and a third eyelid protects its eyes.
life:
Peregrines eat mostly birds, from songbirds to ducks, caught in mid-air. Pigeons are a favourite, and feral pigeons support many city peregrines. Worldwide, an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 bird species, about a fifth of all bird species, are hunted by peregrines somewhere. A peregrine usually hunts from high above, then performs a 'stoop', a steep, wings-tucked dive, striking its prey with its feet or grabbing it.

It often kills with a bite to the neck, using a notch on its beak called a tomial tooth. Males and females often hunt different prey: the smaller, more agile male takes more small birds, while the bigger female can tackle ducks and gulls. Outside the breeding season, peregrines usually hunt alone.
family:
Peregrines usually breed at two or three years old, and pairs often mate for life, returning to the same nest site every year. In courtship, the pair performs acrobatic flights, and the male passes food to the female in mid-air.

They don't build nests. The female lays usually three or four eggs in a scrape on a cliff ledge, or a gravel tray on a building. Both parents incubate, and the chicks fledge after about six weeks.
remarkable: Calculations suggest an ideal falcon could reach about 400 km/h in a low-altitude dive and more at high altitude. The fastest reliably measured peregrine stoops are over 320 km/h, faster than any other animal.
outlook:
The peregrine falcon is listed as Least Concern. In the 1950s to 1970s, it vanished from much of North America and Europe, because pesticides like DDT built up in its body and thinned its eggshells. In eastern North America it disappeared entirely as a breeding bird.

After DDT was banned and thousands of captive-bred young were released, including from city buildings, peregrines recovered. They were removed from the US endangered species list in 1999.
people:
For thousands of years, peregrines have been prized in falconry for their speed and their 'stoop'. Today many cities have webcams on peregrine nests, with millions of viewers following the chicks each spring.

Peregrines are also used to scare pigeons and gulls away from airports and buildings. Both its English and scientific names mean 'wandering falcon', after the long journeys of young birds.
relatives:
The peregrine belongs to the genus Falco, along with kestrels, the gyrfalcon, the prairie falcon and the saker falcon. Falcons were once grouped with hawks and eagles, but genetic studies show they are more closely related to parrots and songbirds.

The peregrine has many subspecies, including the pale Barbary falcon of North Africa and the Middle East, sometimes treated as a separate species.
didYouKnow: In some cities, peregrines hunt at night, using the glow of streetlights to catch migrating birds.

quiz.prompt: What is a peregrine's 'stoop'?
choices: A nest on a cliff ledge
The way it perches with its wings folded across its back
quiz.explanation: In a stoop, the falcon tucks its wings and dives at prey, reaching over 320 km/h.

quiz.prompt: Why did peregrines disappear from much of North America?
choices: Pesticides like DDT thinned their eggshells
quiz.explanation: DDT built up in their bodies and made their eggshells break.

quiz.prompt: Where do many city peregrines nest?
choices: In nests they build from twigs in big trees
quiz.explanation: Tall buildings stand in for the cliff ledges they use in the wild.

charities.name: The Peregrine Fund
charities.blurb: Founded to save the peregrine falcon, it now works to conserve birds of prey worldwide.

name: Aardvark
range: Savannas, grasslands and woodlands across Africa south of the Sahara
tagline: Africa's 'earth pig', a living fossil with tube teeth
lede: With a pig's snout, a rabbit's ears and a kangaroo's tail, the aardvark looks assembled from spare parts. It is the last survivor of an entire order of mammals, digs faster than almost any animal, and its abandoned burrows give shelter to dozens of other species.
home:
Aardvarks live across much of Africa south of the Sahara, wherever there are enough ants and termites and soil soft enough to dig: savannas, grasslands, woodlands and bushland. They avoid very rocky ground and swamp forest, where the water table is too high to burrow.

An aardvark digs several kinds of burrow: shallow ones for quick shelter while feeding, and deep, branching home burrows several metres long, where it sleeps through the heat of the day.
anatomy:
An aardvark is stout and arched, about 1 to 1.3 metres long plus a thick, tapering tail, and weighs up to about 65 kg. Its skin is thick and grey-pink, with sparse, coarse hair. It has long, upright ears, a long snout ending in a disc with the nostrils, and powerful legs. The front feet have four toes and the back feet five, each with a strong, spade-like claw.

Its teeth are unique. They have no enamel and no roots, and each is made of hundreds of thin tubes of dentine bundled together, which keep growing throughout its life. Its sticky tongue can reach about 30 centimetres, and its stomach has a muscular section that grinds food like a bird's gizzard, so it barely chews.
life:
Aardvarks come out at night to feed on ants and termites. They walk zigzag routes with their nose to the ground, sniffing out nests, then rip them open with their claws and lap up the insects with their tongue. Dense hairs around the nostrils and the ability to close them keep out dust and biting insects.

A single aardvark can eat tens of thousands of insects in a night. They are solitary and shy, with keen hearing that warns them of lions, leopards, hyenas and pythons. When threatened, an aardvark can dig itself out of sight in minutes, run off in a zigzag, or fight back with its claws.
family:
Females usually give birth to a single young after a pregnancy of about seven months. The newborn is hairless with floppy ears and pink skin, and stays in the burrow for its first couple of weeks.

It starts following its mother on her nightly foraging trips at a few weeks old, is weaned at about three months, and digs burrows of its own by six months, though it may stay with its mother until the next young is born. Aardvarks live up to 23 years in captivity.
remarkable: The aardvark is the only living member of the order Tubulidentata, 'tube-toothed', a lineage that goes back tens of millions of years in Africa. Its closest living relatives are not anteaters but elephants, manatees, hyraxes and elephant shrews.
outlook:
The aardvark is listed as Least Concern and is widespread, though seldom seen because it is nocturnal and secretive. Some are hunted for meat or killed as farm pests.

Severe droughts, which can wipe out the termites they eat, have killed many aardvarks in southern Africa, and scientists worry about how they'll cope with a hotter, drier climate.
people:
The name comes from Afrikaans and means 'earth pig', because of its burrowing. Its digging annoys farmers, since the holes can damage roads and dams, but aardvarks also control termites.

In some African traditions, parts of the aardvark are used as charms. To many children worldwide, the aardvark is known as the first animal in the dictionary and as Arthur, the cartoon character.
relatives:
Despite similar diets and long snouts, the aardvark is not related to the anteaters of South America or the pangolins of Africa and Asia: all three evolved their insect-eating build separately.

The aardvark belongs to the Afrotheria, a group of mammals that evolved in Africa and includes elephants, manatees, hyraxes, tenrecs and golden moles. Its genus name, Orycteropus, means 'burrowing foot'.
didYouKnow: The aardvark cucumber, a plant that fruits underground, depends on aardvarks: they dig up and eat the fruit, and spread its seeds in their dung.

quiz.prompt: What does the name 'aardvark' mean?
choices: Night digger, from an old Zulu word
quiz.explanation: It comes from Afrikaans and means 'earth pig', because it burrows.

quiz.prompt: What is unusual about the aardvark's teeth?
choices: They're bundles of tubes with no enamel
They're made of keratin, like hair
It grows a new set every year when the old ones wear down
quiz.explanation: Each tooth is made of many thin tubes of dentine, with no enamel or roots, and keeps growing.

quiz.prompt: Which animals are the aardvark's closest living relatives?
quiz.explanation: It belongs to the Afrotheria; its anteater-like build evolved separately.

charities.name: African Wildlife Foundation
charities.blurb: Works across Africa to protect wildlife and wild lands with local communities.

name: Naked Mole-rat
range: Dry grasslands of Kenya, Ethiopia and Somalia in the Horn of Africa
tagline: A wrinkly rodent that lives like an ant colony
lede: Pink, almost hairless and wrinkled like an old sausage, the naked mole-rat breaks most of the rules of being a mammal. It lives in colonies ruled by a single queen, like ants or bees. It can survive 18 minutes without oxygen, feels no pain from acid, rarely gets cancer, and lives for over 37 years.
home:
Naked mole-rats live underground in the hot, dry grasslands of the Horn of Africa, in Kenya, Ethiopia and Somalia. Their tunnel systems can stretch for kilometres, with chambers for nesting, food stores and toilets. The tunnels stay at a fairly steady temperature, but the air inside is poor: crowded with animals and sealed from the surface, it is low in oxygen and high in carbon dioxide.

They rarely come above ground, mainly when a young adult disperses to found a new colony. A single colony's tunnels can cover an area the size of several football pitches, and new tunnels are dug most actively after rain, when the hard soil softens.
anatomy:
A typical naked mole-rat is 8 to 10 centimetres long and weighs only 30 to 35 grams; queens are larger, up to about 80 grams. It has almost no fur, only scattered sensory hairs, and loose, wrinkled skin. Its eyes are tiny and its vision poor.

Its big front teeth stick out in front of its lips, so it can dig with its teeth without getting soil in its mouth. Each tooth can move on its own, like chopsticks. It has small lungs and blood that binds oxygen very well, helping it cope with stale tunnel air.

Its skin lacks the substance that makes acid or chilli sting in other mammals. Its legs are short and thin, and it can run backwards through its tunnels as fast as it runs forwards.
life:
Naked mole-rats eat roots and large underground tubers, which they reach by digging tunnels as a team: one digs with its teeth, others sweep the soil backwards with their feet in a chain, and one kicks it up out of a hole, like a tiny volcano.

A large tuber can feed a colony for months, since they eat the inside and let it regrow. Unlike other mammals, they barely control their own body temperature, which drifts with the temperature of their tunnels. They warm up by huddling or moving to shallower, sun-warmed tunnels.
family:
A colony usually holds about 70 to 80 animals, and sometimes up to 300. Only one female, the queen, breeds, with one to three males. The rest are workers that dig, gather food, care for young and defend the colony against snakes, and larger 'soldiers'.

The queen can have a litter every few months, often of about 10 to 12 pups, and the workers help raise them. When the queen dies, females fight, sometimes to the death, to take her place, and the winner grows longer as her spine lengthens.
remarkable: In experiments, naked mole-rats survived 18 minutes with no oxygen at all, by switching to burning fructose instead of glucose, as plants do. They are also the longest-lived rodent, at over 37 years, and their risk of dying doesn't rise with age the way it does for almost every other mammal.
outlook:
The naked mole-rat is listed as Least Concern. It is common within its range, and its underground life protects it from most threats. It is also widely kept in zoos and laboratories.

Because colonies are so closely related, a disease or a flood could in theory hit a whole group at once, but no serious decline has been recorded.
people:
Scientists study naked mole-rats intensely for clues to ageing, cancer, pain and stroke. Their cells resist forming tumours, partly thanks to a sugar called hyaluronan, and their skin nerves lack a chemical messenger that makes acid and chilli burn.

Researchers hope some of their tricks might one day help people. They're also popular in zoos, where visitors can watch a colony at work in see-through tunnels.
relatives:
Naked mole-rats are rodents, related to porcupines, guinea pigs and chinchillas. They were long grouped with the African mole-rats, or blesmols, but are now placed in their own family, Heterocephalidae.

The only other mammal known to live in queen-ruled colonies like this is a relative, the Damaraland mole-rat of southern Africa.
didYouKnow: A naked mole-rat's front teeth sit outside its lips, so it can dig with its mouth closed.

quiz.prompt: How is a naked mole-rat colony organised?
choices: One queen breeds and the rest are workers
Pairs live alone in their own tunnels
Groups of brothers share a tunnel and swap partners each year
quiz.explanation: Like ants or bees, a single queen breeds while the others work for the colony.

quiz.prompt: How do naked mole-rats survive without oxygen?
quiz.explanation: In experiments they survived 18 minutes with no oxygen by burning fructose, as plants do.

quiz.prompt: How long can a naked mole-rat live?
quiz.explanation: It is the longest-lived rodent, and its risk of death doesn't rise with age.

charities.name: Smithsonian's National Zoo
charities.blurb: Keeps a naked mole-rat colony and supports conservation science worldwide.

name: Honey Badger
range: Most of Africa, Arabia, Iran and Central Asia to India
tagline: The fearless weasel that shrugs off snake bites
lede: The honey badger has a reputation as the most fearless animal on Earth, and it isn't entirely undeserved. It raids beehives, digs up venomous snakes, and sees off lions. Its secret is skin so loose and thick that a predator biting it can't get a firm grip, and the badger can twist around inside it to bite back.
home:
Honey badgers live across most of Africa south of the Sahara, from South Africa's Western Cape to Morocco, and through Arabia, Iran and Central Asia to India.

They live almost everywhere except the driest deserts and the wettest rainforests: savannas, woodlands, scrub, semi-deserts and mountains up to 4,000 metres in Ethiopia. They shelter in burrows they dig themselves, or take over old burrows of aardvarks and warthogs, or termite mounds.
anatomy:
The honey badger is the largest land member of the weasel family in Africa, 55 to 77 centimetres long and up to 16 kg, with males larger than females. It has a long, broad, thick-set body, short legs, a small flat head and tiny ears.

Its coat is black underneath, with a wide grey-white cape from the top of the head to the tail, a pattern thought to warn predators off. Its skin is very loose and about 6 millimetres thick around the neck. Its front claws, up to 4 centimetres long, are powerful digging tools, and it has a pouch that releases a foul-smelling liquid.
life:
Honey badgers eat almost anything. They dig up rodents, scorpions, insect larvae and reptiles, and also eat frogs, tortoises, birds, eggs, carrion, berries and roots. They break into beehives for the larvae and honey, enduring hundreds of stings. They are famous for eating snakes, including cobras and puff adders. A bitten badger may collapse, apparently from the venom, then wake up and carry on eating.

Most live and forage alone, travelling long distances each day, and in the Serengeti they are active mostly at night in the dry season and more by day in the wet. It also follows other predators, such as jackals and snake eagles, to share in their kills or scraps.
family:
Honey badgers have no fixed breeding season. After a pregnancy of about 50 to 70 days, the female gives birth to one or two cubs in a burrow lined with grass. She often moves them to a new burrow every few days.

The cubs stay with their mother for more than a year, sometimes up to 16 months, learning where to find food and how to deal with dangerous prey. In captivity, honey badgers have lived for about 24 years.
remarkable: Honey badgers are clever escape artists. In a well-known case at a wildlife rehabilitation centre in South Africa, a captive honey badger called Stoffel learned to open gates, stack objects and use tools to climb out of his enclosure.
outlook:
The honey badger is listed as Least Concern because of its huge range and its ability to live in many habitats. In some places, though, it is killed by beekeepers and poultry farmers, often with poison and traps.

Raising hives on stands the badgers can't climb has helped beekeepers in South Africa protect both bees and badgers. Hunters also take them for traditional medicine in some areas, and they are caught in traps set for other animals. They are thought to be rare in parts of their Asian range.
people:
The honey badger became an internet celebrity after a viral video in 2011, and it has appeared as a mascot and nickname for tough soldiers and sports teams. In parts of Africa and Asia it is believed to have magical properties.

It is often said to team up with a bird, the greater honeyguide, which leads it to bees' nests. That partnership is well documented between honeyguides and people, but scientists have found little good evidence that it happens with honey badgers.
relatives:
The honey badger is the only living species in its own subfamily, Mellivorinae, within the weasel family.

Despite its name, it isn't closely related to European or American badgers; its closest relatives may be the martens. The lineage goes back at least 7 million years, with extinct relatives known from fossils in South Africa, Italy, Pakistan and Chad.
didYouKnow: Honey badgers have been seen using logs and rocks as ladders to climb out of enclosures.

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: Up to about 24 years in captivity

quiz.prompt: What helps a honey badger escape a predator's bite?
choices: Its very fast running speed across open ground
quiz.explanation: Its loose skin is hard to grip, and it can twist around inside it to bite back.

quiz.prompt: What happens when a venomous snake bites a honey badger?
choices: It becomes paralysed for days and has to be fed by its mother
quiz.explanation: Bitten badgers have been seen collapsing, then waking and carrying on.

quiz.prompt: How do beekeepers protect hives from honey badgers?
choices: Raising hives on stands badgers can't climb
quiz.explanation: Hives on raised stands protect both bees and badgers.

charities.name: Endangered Wildlife Trust
charities.blurb: A South African conservation organisation that works on wildlife conflicts with farmers, among much else.

name: Capybara
range: Rivers, lakes and wetlands in every South American country except Chile
tagline: The giant, unbothered rodent of the riverbank
lede: The capybara is the largest rodent in the world, a guinea pig the size of a big dog, and famously relaxed. It spends hot afternoons wallowing in rivers, lets birds perch on its back, and lives in social groups that bark, purr and whistle to each other.
home:
Capybaras live in every country in South America except Chile, east of the Andes. They are never far from fresh water: rivers, lakes, ponds, swamps, marshes and reservoirs, in seasonally flooded savannas, wetlands such as Brazil's Pantanal and Venezuela's llanos, and along rivers through rainforest.

They mostly live in lowlands, and adapt well to farmland and cattle ranches, and even city parks and lakes.
anatomy:
A capybara has a heavy, barrel-shaped body, short legs and a broad, blunt head, with no visible tail. Adults weigh 35 to 66 kg and stand about 50 to 60 centimetres at the shoulder. Its coarse fur is reddish brown above and yellowish brown below, and it has sweat glands in its skin, unusual for a rodent.

Its feet are slightly webbed, and its eyes, ears and nostrils sit high on its head, so it can hide underwater with just its face showing, like a hippo. Males have a large, dark scent gland on top of the snout, called a morrillo, which they rub on grass and bushes to mark territory.
life:
Capybaras are grazers, eating mainly grasses and water plants, as well as fruit and bark. They are choosy, often eating one kind of plant while ignoring others around it.

To get the most out of tough grass, they eat some of their own droppings, which contain bacteria that help digest it, and they bring food back up to chew again, like cows. They rest on land in the morning, cool off in the water during the hot early afternoon, and graze from late afternoon through the night.

They are superb swimmers and can stay underwater for up to five minutes to escape danger. Capybaras are very vocal, using barks to warn of danger, purrs between friends, and whistles and clicks to keep in touch while grazing.
family:
Capybaras usually live in groups of 10 to 20, with a few adult males, several adult females and their young; in the dry season, when water is scarce, groups can swell to 50 or 100. A dominant male leads the group. A female lets males know she is ready to mate by whistling through her nose, and capybaras mate only in water.

After about 150 days, she gives birth to an average of four pups, which can walk and graze within days. Young are cared for by all the group's females, and may nurse from any of them.
remarkable: Capybaras have a famously calm relationship with other animals. Birds such as cattle tyrants and caracaras ride on their backs, picking off ticks and catching insects they flush from the grass, and the capybaras simply carry on grazing.
outlook:
The capybara is listed as Least Concern, and is common across much of its range. It is hunted for meat and leather in some areas, and in parts of Venezuela it is raised on ranches.

Their main natural predators are jaguars, pumas, ocelots, caimans, anacondas and eagles; in the wild, few live beyond four years. Wetland drainage for farming is a threat in some places, but capybaras breed quickly, and populations bounce back when hunting is controlled.
people:
In Venezuela, capybara meat is a traditional dish at Easter. In the 16th century, local clergy asked the Vatican whether they could eat it during Lent, when meat was forbidden, and because it lives in water, it was allowed to be treated as fish.

Capybaras have become internet stars thanks to their calm nature, and have spread into city parks in Brazil and Argentina, sometimes to the dismay of residents.
relatives:
The capybara is a cavy, related to guinea pigs and rock cavies, and more distantly to agoutis, chinchillas and nutria.

Its only close living relative is the lesser capybara of Panama, Colombia and Venezuela. Its ancestors were even bigger: extinct relatives such as Phugatherium were larger than today's capybara.
didYouKnow: The name capybara comes from a Tupi word often translated as 'one who eats slender leaves'.

quiz.prompt: Why are a capybara's eyes, ears and nostrils high on its head?
choices: So it can hide underwater with only its face showing
To keep its face dry when it rains in the forest
quiz.explanation: Like a hippo, it can lie almost completely submerged.

quiz.prompt: Where do capybaras mate?
quiz.explanation: Capybaras mate only in water.

quiz.prompt: How does a capybara get more out of tough grass?
choices: It eats some of its own droppings
It soaks the grass in water first
It lets birds peck the tough stems off for it
quiz.explanation: Its droppings contain helpful gut bacteria, and it also brings food back up to chew again.

charities.name: World Wildlife Fund
charities.blurb: Works to protect South American wetlands such as the Pantanal, home to capybaras and jaguars.

name: Giant Anteater
range: Grasslands and forests from Honduras to Bolivia and northern Argentina
tagline: A tongue 60 cm long and no teeth at all
lede: The giant anteater has no teeth, can barely open its mouth, and lives almost entirely on ants and termites. To eat enough, it flicks a sticky tongue up to 60 centimetres long in and out of a nest well over a hundred times a minute, then moves on before the soldiers can fight back.
home:
Giant anteaters live in Central and South America, from Honduras to Bolivia and northern Argentina, east of the Andes. They use many habitats, including grasslands, savannas, wetlands such as the Pantanal and rainforest, often foraging in the open and resting in the shade of forest when it's hot. They have disappeared from Uruguay, Belize, El Salvador and Guatemala and parts of Costa Rica.

Fossils show they once lived as far north as Sonora, Mexico. In the hot season they are active mainly in the cool of the evening and night, and in colder places they switch to feeding by day.
anatomy:
The giant anteater is the largest of the four anteater species, 1.8 to 2.2 metres long including its huge, bushy tail, and weighing 27 to 50 kg. Its coat is grizzled grey and brown, with a bold black stripe edged in white running diagonally from its chest over its shoulders.

Its long, narrow head ends in a tiny mouth. It has no teeth at all, and its jaw works by rotating the two halves of the lower jaw rather than opening wide. Its front feet carry long, curved claws, up to 10 centimetres, so it walks on its knuckles to keep them sharp. Its body temperature is low for a mammal, about 33 °C, which saves energy on its low-calorie diet.
life:
Giant anteaters feed mostly on ants and termites, eating up to 30,000 insects a day. They find nests by smell, which is about 40 times more sensitive than ours, tear them open with their claws and lap up the insects with their tongue, coated in sticky saliva.

Tiny backward-pointing spines on the tongue help hold the insects. An anteater feeds at each nest for only a minute or so, leaving it intact to recover, and visits many nests a day.

They are mostly solitary, and when cornered they rear up on their hind legs and slash with their claws, strong enough to fend off a jaguar. It sleeps up to 15 hours a day in a shallow hollow, covering itself with its bushy tail like a blanket.
family:
Females give birth to a single pup after a pregnancy of about six months. The pup is born with a full coat that matches its mother's.

It rides on its mother's back for up to a year, lying along her body so that its black and white stripe lines up with hers, making mother and pup look like one animal to a predator. Young anteaters become independent at about two years old.
remarkable: To swallow its prey without chewing, the anteater crushes the insects against the roof of its mouth and in a muscular stomach, with help from the sand and small stones it swallows along the way.
outlook:
The giant anteater is listed as Vulnerable. It has disappeared from much of its former range because of habitat loss to farming, large fires in grasslands, road traffic and hunting.

Its slow breeding makes it hard for populations to recover. Many live in protected areas, and reintroduction programmes in Argentina's Iberá wetlands have brought them back to places they had vanished from.
people:
With its unusual look, the giant anteater appears in the stories and art of pre-Columbian peoples.

Today it is hunted for meat or fur in some places, and killed by dogs and on roads. In Brazil, it is a familiar sight on roadsides in the Cerrado grasslands, where collisions with vehicles kill large numbers each year.
relatives:
Anteaters are related to sloths; together they form the order Pilosa. Armadillos are their next closest relatives.

The giant anteater is the only member of its genus, and the only living anteater that lives mainly on the ground; the other three species, the two tamanduas and the silky anteater, live mostly in trees. Its genus name, Myrmecophaga, means 'anteater' in Greek.
didYouKnow: A giant anteater's tongue can flick in and out of its mouth about 150 times a minute.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Ants and termites, up to 30,000 a day

quiz.prompt: Why does a giant anteater only feed at a nest for a minute or so?
choices: To leave the nest intact and avoid soldier insects
It's always being chased by jaguars while it eats
quiz.explanation: It eats a little from many nests, leaving each one to recover.

quiz.prompt: How does a giant anteater pup hide from predators?
choices: Its stripe lines up with its mother's
It hides inside a hollow termite mound
quiz.explanation: Riding on her back, the pup blends into her outline so they look like one animal.

quiz.prompt: Why does a giant anteater walk on its knuckles?
choices: To keep its long front claws sharp
Because its feet have no pads
quiz.explanation: Walking on its knuckles protects its long digging claws.

charities.name: World Wildlife Fund
charities.blurb: Works to protect South America's grasslands and forests, including the Cerrado and Pantanal.

name: American Bullfrog
range: Ponds, lakes and swamps of eastern North America, introduced worldwide
tagline: A frog that bellows like a bull and swallows bats
lede: On summer nights the deep, droning call of the male bullfrog rolls across North American ponds, sounding uncannily like a distant bull. Behind that voice is a big, hungry frog that will try to eat almost anything that fits in its mouth, and quite a few things that barely do.
home:
The bullfrog is native to eastern North America and is common in every US state east of the Mississippi. Its natural range runs from the Canadian Maritime Provinces west to Idaho and Texas, and north to Michigan, Minnesota and Montana. It favours large, permanent water: swamps, ponds and lakes, but also garden pools, koi ponds, canals, ditches, reservoirs and culverts.

People have carried it far beyond that range. It now lives across much of the western United States and in more than 40 countries, from Mexico, Cuba and Brazil to Belgium, Italy, China, Japan and South Korea, often after escaping from frog farms or being released on purpose.
anatomy:
This is the largest true frog in North America. Adults usually measure 9 to 15 centimetres from snout to vent, and big individuals weigh up to 500 g, with a few recorded at 800 g and 20 centimetres. The back is olive green, plain or mottled with greyish brown, and the belly is off-white blotched with yellow or grey.

The eye is prominent with a brown iris and a horizontal pupil. The round eardrum sits just behind the eye. In males it is larger than the eye, while in females it is about the same size, and males also have yellow throats. The front legs are short and sturdy, the hind legs long, and all the back toes but the fourth are webbed.
life:
